titre: What trees don't tell each other underground
accroche: Books and documentaries describe a forest linked by a fungal network in which trees help one another. A scientific re-examination has reopened the case.
contenu_vulgarise:
For about a decade, one image has circulated widely, popularized by bestselling books and documentaries. Beneath the forest litter, a network of fungi is said to link the roots of trees into a “wood wide web,” a forest that trades resources and warns of danger. The phrase rests on a very real phenomenon, long documented by mycology, the mycorrhiza: an association between a plant's roots and a fungus, in which the fungus spreads a network of filaments (the mycelium) through the soil in exchange for sugars produced by the tree's photosynthesis.

## What a 2023 re-examination actually found

The next step, the one that makes the story so successful, is to say that this mycelium links several trees to one another in a common mycorrhizal network able to transfer resources and warning signals. In 2023, in Nature Ecology & Evolution, the biologists Justine Karst, Melanie Jones and Jason Hoeksema reopened the studies on which this claim is founded. Of the work that tried to map genetically a network actually linking trees in a forest, they find only five in all, covering just two types of forest, two tree species and three fungal species. Going back over 26 field studies on resource transfer, they find that, in the most tightly controlled experiments, fewer than 20% show that a young tree connected to the network does better than an isolated tree. In the others, it does the same or worse. As for the idea that trees send each other warning signals through this network, it rests on a single study, conducted in a greenhouse and never reproduced in a real forest.

## A citation bias that feeds on itself

The three authors also point to a subtler phenomenon. Over successive citations, the articles that relay these results exaggerate their reach, and this drift worsens with time. None of this erases the existence of mycorrhizae themselves, nor the very first studies that launched the idea in the 1990s, showing a measurable transfer of carbon between a Douglas fir and a birch linked by the same fungi. What the 2023 re-examination corrects is the leap made afterward, from that isolated observation to the picture of a network-forest that consciously cooperates, a leap that field data do not yet support.

What remains is an open question rather than a clear-cut answer: the authors of the re-examination do not conclude that trees never communicate this way, but that science has not, so far, gathered enough evidence to assert it as broadly as books and documentaries tell it.

repere.texte: Of twenty-six field studies examining resource transfer between trees via a mycorrhizal network, fewer than 20% show, in the most tightly controlled experiments, that a connected young tree fares better than an isolated one.
repere.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, “Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests,” Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023

carte.punch: Fewer than 20% of the most tightly controlled field experiments show a tree helped by the network.
carte.idee: Books and documentaries describe a forest linked by a fungal network in which trees help one another. A 2023 re-examination of 26 field studies rarely confirms it, and only five studies have mapped such a network between trees in a forest.
carte.source_courte: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; open access. Takes stock of what carbon transfer between trees via mycorrhizae really establishes, without giving in to the sensational story.

quiz.question: What exactly does the 2023 re-examination published in Nature Ecology & Evolution correct?
choix: That mycorrhizae, the association between roots and fungi, do not exist in forest soils
That the carbon transfer measured in 1997 between a fir and a birch was entirely made up
That the evidence for real sharing of resources and warning signals between trees is far thinner than advertised
That trees have no roots capable of making contact with a fungus
quiz.explication: The existence of mycorrhizae is not in question: it is the leap to a network that would link trees so that they cooperate consciously that field data do not yet support, for lack of solid, numerous studies on the subject.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many studies that genetically mapped a mycorrhizal network actually linking trees in a forest does the 2023 re-examination rely on?
choix: Five studies in all, covering only two types of forest
More than a hundred studies, conducted on every continent
No field studies, only computer simulations
Twenty-six studies, all conducted in the same Canadian forest
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Karst, Jones and Hoeksema count only five studies that genetically mapped such a network in a forest, covering two types of forest, two tree species and three fungal species.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the idea that trees send each other warning signals through the mycorrhizal network rest on?
choix: On an observation repeated in several dozen different forests
On a single study, conducted in a greenhouse and never reproduced in a real forest
On the same data as the carbon transfer measured in 1997
On a consensus established since the 1990s by classical mycology
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The idea of a warning signal passed along the network rests on a single study conducted in a greenhouse, never reproduced under real forest conditions.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2023 re-examination identify as a phenomenon aggravating the spread of the wood wide web story?
choix: Deliberate falsification of the data by the first authors in 1997
A confusion between mycorrhizae and soil bacteria
A citation bias, which exaggerates the reach of results as they are picked up again and again
A lack of funding that has prevented any field study since 1997
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The three authors point to a citation bias: over successive citations, the articles that relay these results exaggerate their reach, a drift that worsens with time.
